chapters.title: Chapter 4: Adding a Risk-Free Asset: The Capital Market Line

lessons.title: The Tangency Portfolio and Its Link to the Sharpe Ratio

children.text: Lesson 1 scanned a handful of points on the five-stock frontier and found the Sharpe ratio peaking somewhere between the 16.00% and 16.50% return points, without pinning down exactly where. This lesson finds that exact point, and shows why it is not just one interesting portfolio among many, but arguably the single most important portfolio on the entire frontier.

body.text: The tangency portfolio is the one point on the efficient frontier where a line from the risk-free rate just touches the curve, tangent to it, rather than crossing through it. It is the single risky portfolio with the highest possible Sharpe ratio in the entire universe of assets you are considering.

children.text: Picture every possible CAL from Lesson 1, one line for every possible choice of risky portfolio P on the frontier, all pivoting from the same point, (0, Rf). Most of these lines cross INTO the frontier curve and back out, meaning some portfolio further along the curve beats that particular line at some risk levels. Exactly one line only ever touches the curve, at a single point, without crossing it anywhere. That line is the steepest one achievable, and the point where it touches is the tangency portfolio.

body.caption: Maximize the Sharpe ratio directly, over every portfolio with weights summing to 1.

children.text: Solved the same way as Lesson 3 of Chapter 3, with a Lagrangian and a gradient set to zero, this produces its own closed form. The only new ingredient is that expected returns now enter as EXCESS returns over the risk-free rate, mu minus Rf, rather than raw expected returns.

body.caption: The tangency portfolio's weights: the same inverse-covariance machinery as the minimum-variance formula, now pointed at excess returns instead of a plain vector of ones.

body.label: Tangency portfolio: return, risk, and Sharpe ratio
body.context: Confirms Lesson 1's scan exactly: the true peak sits between the 16.00% and 16.50% frontier points, precisely at 16.23%.

body.text: 0.6337 is not dramatically higher than the 0.6333 already found at the 16.00% frontier point back in Lesson 1. That is normal: near the true peak of any smooth curve, the curve is close to flat, so nearby points score almost as well as the exact maximum. The formula's real value is certainty, not a large numeric improvement. It tells you precisely where the peak is, rather than leaving you to guess how close a scanned point actually came.

children.text: Why This Portfolio Is the Only One That Matters

Here is the genuinely surprising conclusion this chapter has been building toward. Every investor prefers a steeper CAL to a flatter one, since it delivers more return at every risk level. The tangency portfolio produces the single steepest CAL achievable from this set of assets. That means EVERY investor, no matter how aggressive or conservative, should hold the exact same risky portfolio, this one, and differ ONLY in how much weight y they place on it versus the risk-free asset.

body.caption: Same tangency portfolio, different investors, different y

body.text: All three investors in that table hold TCS, Maruti Suzuki, HDFC Bank, HUL, and Reliance in the exact same RELATIVE proportions, 27.29 : 25.32 : 18.19 : 16.88 : 12.32. Only the total amount allocated to that mix, versus the risk-free asset, changes. This result depends entirely on every investor sharing the same expected returns, variances, and covariances. Real investors disagree on all three, which is one reason real portfolios do not actually converge on one universal mix. Lesson 4 of this chapter builds directly on this result to arrive at the Capital Asset Pricing Model.

body.title: Solve a two-asset tangency portfolio
body.prompt: Two uncorrelated assets: Var1 = 10, Var2 = 10, Cov12 = 0, mu1 = 15%, mu2 = 10%, Rf = 5%. What is the tangency portfolio's weight in Asset 1?
body.explanation: With no correlation, Sigma-inverse is just 1/Var on each diagonal. Excess returns are 10% and 5%. Unnormalized weights: 10/10 = 1.0 for Asset 1, 5/10 = 0.5 for Asset 2. Normalizing: 1.0 / (1.0 + 0.5) = 0.667, or 66.7%.

body.title: The one-fund implication
body.question: Two investors share the same universe of risky assets, the same expected returns, and the same covariance matrix, but one is far more risk-tolerant than the other. According to this lesson, how should their RISKY holdings differ?
options: The risk-tolerant investor should hold a completely different mix of risky assets, tilted toward the highest-return names
Their risky holdings should have the identical relative composition, the tangency portfolio; only the SIZE of the allocation to it, versus the risk-free asset, should differ
The risk-tolerant investor should hold only the minimum-variance portfolio, scaled up with leverage
There is no way to compare their optimal holdings without more information
body.explanation: Since the tangency portfolio produces the single steepest CAL, both investors should want the exact same risky mix, the tangency portfolio, and adjust only y, the proportion allocated to it versus the risk-free asset, to match their own risk tolerance. This is the one-fund result underlying this lesson.

cards.definition: The unique risky portfolio on the efficient frontier where the Capital Allocation Line is tangent to the frontier, maximizing the Sharpe ratio.
wT = Sigma-inverse x (mu - Rf x 1), normalized to sum to 1. The minimum-variance formula's structure, applied to excess returns instead of a vector of ones.

The conclusion that every investor, regardless of risk tolerance, should hold the same risky portfolio (the tangency portfolio), differing only in how much is allocated to it versus the risk-free asset.

points: The tangency portfolio is the single point on the efficient frontier where a line from the risk-free rate touches the curve without crossing it, maximizing the Sharpe ratio.
It has its own closed-form formula, wT = Sigma-inverse x (mu minus Rf x 1), normalized to sum to 1, structurally identical to the minimum-variance formula but built from excess returns.
Applied to the five-stock universe, the exact tangency portfolio sits at 16.23% return and 15.35% risk, a Sharpe ratio of 0.6337, confirming Lesson 1's scanned estimate precisely.

Because it produces the single steepest possible CAL, every investor sharing the same expectations should hold the tangency portfolio in identical relative proportions, adjusting only how much of their capital sits in it versus the risk-free asset.
This striking result depends entirely on every investor agreeing on expected returns, variances, and covariances, an assumption real markets do not actually satisfy.
This one-fund result is the direct foundation for Lesson 4's Capital Asset Pricing Model, later in this chapter.
